title: Naman Dhir Warns Against Complacency as India Take 2-1 Lead Into Hyderabad
excerpt: The 26-year-old all-rounder, India's leading wicket-taker in the West Indies T20I series, says the visitors are too dangerous in this format for India to ease off in the fourth match.
body:
• India lead the five-match T20I series against the West Indies 2-1 heading into the fourth match in Hyderabad on October 14.
  • Naman Dhir, 26, is India's leading wicket-taker in the series with five wickets, including 3 for 31 on debut in Lucknow and 2 for 39 in Indore.
  • Dhir says his immediate priority is scoring more runs from his No. 6 or 7 role, even as he works toward becoming a genuine all-rounder.
  • India defended 223 in Indore to win by 14 runs; a win in Hyderabad seals the series with a match to spare.

Naman Dhir has warned that India cannot afford any drop in intensity despite holding a 2-1 lead over the West Indies, as the five-match T20I series moves to Hyderabad for the fourth match on Wednesday. Speaking ahead of the game, the 26-year-old all-rounder described the visitors as a dangerous side in the shortest format and said the lesson of the series so far was that no lead is safe, according to IANS.

"You can't be complacent at any stage of the series. Yes, we are 2-1 up, but we'll still play the game with the same intensity."

— Naman Dhir, India all-rounder

A Bowler by Accident of Opportunity

Dhir's series has been defined by an unlikely stat line: the batting all-rounder is India's leading wicket-taker with five wickets. He took 3 for 31 on his T20I debut in Lucknow, then added 2 for 39 in Indore, dismissing Shimron Hetmyer and Kamil Pooran during the West Indies' chase of 224 as India defended 223 to win by 14 runs and take the series lead. Each of his wickets, he noted with some amusement, has come after he conceded a six — a pattern he hopes to break in Hyderabad, where the larger ground, compared with Indore's Holkar Stadium, gives spinners more margin.

He credits his batting background for the bowling returns: reading a batter's stance, backlift and guard helps him anticipate shots and adjust line, length and pace. He has been working on those details with head coach Gautam Gambhir and the support staff through the series.

The Role He Has Been Given

Dhir's own assessment of his job is specific. Team management has told him he will bat at No. 6 or 7 depending on the situation, and bowl two or three economical overs when needed, as he explained on JioStar's Haier Cricket Live, reported by MyKhel. The bowling load is partly a quirk of structure: the IPL's Impact Player rule means he bowls far less for Mumbai Indians than he has since his schooldays, even though he describes himself as a batting all-rounder who enjoys bowling.

His route here ran through domestic form — 655 runs at a strike rate above 217 in the Sher-e-Punjab T20 League, including 173 off 64 balls, followed by consistent seasons for Punjab and Mumbai Indians, according to The Sports Tak. He made his ODI debut in late September and moved quickly into the T20I side.

What Comes Next

Dhir was candid that the batting half of his brief is unfulfilled: he had an opportunity in Indore and did not capitalise on it, and he says contributing more with the bat is his immediate priority even though his stated ambition is to be a genuine all-rounder. Hyderabad offers the next test of both halves — a series-clinching win is available if India hold their nerve, and two matches remain for Dhir to turn a promising first series into a settled place in the side.
